resources.abstract: The latest version of the ISO 26262 standard from 2016 represents the state of the art for a safety-guided development of safety-critical electric/electronic vehicle systems. These vehicle systems include advanced driver assistance systems and vehicle guidance systems. The development process proposed in the ISO 26262 standard is based upon multiple V-models, and defines activities and work products for each process step. In many of these process steps, scenario based approaches can be applied to achieve the defined work products for the development of automated driving functions. To accomplish the work products of different process steps, scenarios have to focus on various aspects like a human understandable notation or a description via state variables. This leads to contradictory requirements regarding the level of detail and way of notation for the representation of scenarios. In this paper, the authors discuss requirements for the representation of scenarios in different process steps defined by the ISO 26262 standard, propose a consistent terminology based on prior publications for the identified levels of abstraction, and demonstrate how scenarios can be systematically evolved along the phases of the development process outlined in the ISO 26262 standard.

resources.abstract: Preventing and mitigating high severity collisions is one of the main opportunities for Automated Driving Systems (ADS) to improve road safety. This study evaluated the Waymo Driver's performance within real-world fatal collision scenarios that occurred in a specific operational design domain (ODD). To address the rare nature of high-severity collisions, this paper describes the addition of novel techniques to established safety impact assessment methodologies. A census of fatal, human-involved collisions was examined for years 2008 through 2017 for Chandler, AZ, which overlaps the current geographic ODD of the Waymo One fully automated ride-hailing service. Crash reconstructions were performed on all available fatal collisions that involved a passenger vehicle as one of the first collision partners and an available map in this ODD to determine the pre-impact kinematics of the vehicles involved in the original crashes. The final dataset consisted of a total of 72 crashes and 91 vehicle actors (52 initiators and 39 responders) for simulations. Next, a novel counterfactual "what-if'' simulation method was developed to synthetically replace human-driven crash participants one at a time with the Waymo Driver. This study focused on the Waymo Driver's performance when replacing one of the first two collision partners. The results of these simulations showed that the Waymo Driver was successful in avoiding all collisions when replacing the crash initiator, that is, the road user who made the initial, unexpected maneuver leading to a collision. Replacing the driver reacting (the responder) to the actions of the crash initiator with the Waymo Driver resulted in an estimated 82% of simulations where a collision was prevented and an additional 10% of simulations where the collision severity was mitigated (reduction in crash-level serious injury risk). The remaining 8% of simulations with the Waymo Driver in the responder role had a similar outcome to the original collision. All of these "unchanged" collisions involved both the original vehicle and the Waymo Driver being struck in the rear in a front-to-rear configuration. These results demonstrate the potential of fully automated driving systems to improve traffic safety compared to the performance of the humans originally involved in the collisions. The findings also highlight the major importance of driving behaviors that prevent entering a conflict situation (e.g. maintaining safe time gaps and not surprising other road users). However, methodological challenges in performing single instance counterfactual simulations based solely on police report data and uncertainty in ADS performance may result in variable performance, requiring additional analysis and supplemental methodologies. This study's methods provide insights on rare, severe events that would otherwise only be experienced after operating in extreme real-world driving distances (many billions of driving miles).

techniques.name: CycloneDX Machine Learning Bill of Materials
techniques.description: A CycloneDX ML-BOM (machine-learning bill of materials) is a machine-readable inventory of what a model is made of, written in the CycloneDX standard (ECMA-424) so that tools as well as people can check it. It applies the software bill of materials, a structured list of the components in a piece of software, to models: the model is declared as a component of type machine-learning-model with its identifiers, version, supplier, licence and file hashes, together with the base models it was derived from (its pedigree), the datasets used to train and evaluate it with their source, classification and owners, the libraries it depends on, and an optional structured model card giving its task, architecture, performance metrics, intended uses and known limitations. The BOM is written at release, by hand or with a generator that reads the model's repository and metadata, checked against the CycloneDX schema, and can be signed. Consumers then query it, for example to find every deployed model that uses a dataset or library found to be compromised, or to check a supplier's declared datasets and licences before purchase. Unlike a model card or datasheet, written for people to read, or an experiment log or data version history, which stay with the team that built the model, it is a parts list in a fixed schema that travels with the model and can be matched against vulnerability records and file hashes, but it records what its author declares and verifies none of it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank keeps an ML-BOM for every deployed model, recording each base model by its Hugging Face package URL and revision, the fine-tuning datasets, the framework libraries and the file hashes. When a compromised base-model release or a vulnerability in a model-loading library is announced, its security team queries the BOMs to list the affected deployments within hours and decides which to withdraw or patch.

A hospital trust buying a diagnostic imaging model requires the supplier to deliver a signed ML-BOM with each version. Before the model enters clinical evaluation, the acceptance team checks the BOM's signature, compares its file hashes with the delivered files and checks the listed libraries against known-vulnerability records.

A government department procuring a document-classification model asks bidders for an ML-BOM whose model-card and dataset fields declare each training and evaluation dataset with its source, licence and owner, and the model's known technical limitations. Its assessors and later its auditors read and query these declarations to compare bids and to check what the chosen supplier said it used.

A software company generates an ML-BOM for each release of its customer-support assistant with an open-source generator, recording the base and embedding models, the quantised model file and the framework libraries with hashes. Its security team compares each new BOM with the previous release's to catch an unreviewed change of base model or library before the release ships.

limitations.description: It records what its author declares. Nothing in the format checks that the listed datasets were the ones used, that the model-card fields are true or that the list is complete, so a BOM is evidence that a disclosure was made, not that it is accurate. Hashes and a signature show that the document and the files it lists have not changed since it was written, which is a different thing.

Almost every field is optional: ECMA-424 requires a component's type and name and little else, so a BOM can pass schema validation while saying almost nothing. In a 2026 preprint that generated ML-BOMs with one open-source tool for about 98,000 Hugging Face models, every BOM had the required fields, but only 39% named a dataset, 17% listed technical limitations and 0.2% had a meaningful description. A claim needs the fields it relies on to be checked, not only schema validity.

Generators can fill only what they can read: hub metadata, model-card text and configuration files. Training data, fine-tuning history and settings that the publisher never wrote down stay empty, and for a model bought from a supplier the BOM is only as complete as the supplier chooses to make it.

Each BOM describes one version of one model. Fine-tuning, quantisation, a new framework release or a changed dataset needs a new BOM, and the ability to answer 'which of our models use this component?' when a compromise is disclosed depends on BOMs being regenerated and kept for every deployed version, which is a standing process cost rather than a one-off task.

techniques.name: Malicious Model-File Scanning
techniques.description: Malicious model-file scanning checks a downloaded or received model file for code that would run when the file is loaded, without loading it. Several common ways of saving (serialising) models can carry such code, above all Python's pickle format, the default for PyTorch checkpoints and the usual format for scikit-learn models, whose files can instruct the loader to import and call any Python function, so that loading an untrusted file can hand an attacker control of the machine; since version 2.6 PyTorch's own loader by default allows only a small set of known-safe functions, but some libraries switch that off to load their models. The named method is ModelScan, an open-source scanner from Protect AI, which chooses a check by file extension and reads the file as data: for pickle-based files it lists the functions the file would import and compares them with a graded list of unsafe ones, such as the os, subprocess and socket modules and Python's built-in eval and exec, and for Keras and TensorFlow files it flags Lambda layers, which hold arbitrary Python, and operations that read or write files. It reports each finding with a severity from critical to low and exits with a non-zero code when it finds any, so a pipeline can stop the file before anything loads it. The evidence is a record that no listed unsafe call was found in the files scanned; unlike data-poisoning detection it examines the saved file rather than the training data, and it shows neither that the file is safe, nor how the model behaves, nor who produced the file.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's machine-learning platform team adds a ModelScan step to the job that imports models from public hubs into its internal registry. A critical or high-severity finding stops the import and opens a ticket for the security team, which decides whether the third-party checkpoint may enter the registry at all.

A university's research-computing service scans every checkpoint users upload to shared GPU storage, including PyTorch .pt files and scikit-learn models saved with joblib, before jobs on nodes shared between research groups can load them, and quarantines any file with a critical finding until its owner explains the flagged imports.

A manufacturer's operational-technology security team scans each Keras visual-inspection model delivered by an outside contractor before it is copied to factory edge devices. A flagged Lambda layer is accepted only after the contractor supplies the layer's source code and an engineer confirms that it does nothing beyond resizing and normalising images.

limitations.description: It finds only what is on its list. In a peer-reviewed comparison ModelScan missed 9 of 84 known malicious models: five called functions not on its list (the authors' own example wrote files through Python's pathlib module instead of open), three loaded a further payload at run time, for example through numpy.load, and one hid its payload after an early stop instruction, where the scanner stopped reading. A clean scan shows that no known pattern was found, not that the file is safe.

Attackers adapt faster than the list. A peer-reviewed study (2026) found 22 routes by which five frameworks load pickled data, 19 of which evaded all four scanners it tested, ModelScan included, and in a 2026 preprint ModelScan detected none of 3,000 new attack files. A scan is only as current as the scanner release and unsafe list it ran with.

It checks only the files and formats it recognises, chosen by file extension, and skips the rest, so a pass can cover only some of what the loader will open. Showing that a model was checked needs the list of skipped files (ModelScan can print it) and a check that every file the loading code reads was among those scanned.

Findings need judgement. Every Keras Lambda layer is flagged, though Lambda layers are meant for ordinary pre- and post-processing, and benign models from some libraries import functions that pickle scanners treat as suspicious (one peer-reviewed study describes a widely downloaded model flagged this way). Someone able to read the flagged imports or layer code, or to question the model's author, has to decide each case.

It looks for code that runs on load, not for harmful behaviour in the weights. A model whose weights were altered to carry a backdoor, or that was trained on poisoned data, contains no unsafe call and scans clean, as does any file in a format that cannot hold code, such as safetensors; ModelScan's own documentation notes that weights can be manipulated in such formats. Backdoor and poisoning checks are separate techniques.

techniques.name: Model Signing
techniques.description: Model signing lets the publisher of a machine-learning model attach a cryptographic signature to the model's files, so that anyone who later loads them can check who released them and that no file has changed since. Under the Open Source Security Foundation's Model Signing (OMS) specification and its reference tool, model-signing, the publisher computes a hash (a short fingerprint that changes if a single byte of the file changes) of every file in the model directory, such as weights, configuration, tokeniser and any dataset files kept with them, lists the hashes in a sorted manifest and signs the manifest, producing a detached signature file kept beside the model. The signature can be made with the publisher's own key, with a certificate from an organisation's certificate authority, or through Sigstore, which issues a short-lived certificate tied to a verified online identity, such as a person's account or a build pipeline's, and records each signing event in a transparency log, an append-only record that can be inspected afterwards. Before loading, the consumer verifies the signature against the signer it expects, recomputes every hash and rejects the model if any listed file differs or is missing or, unless that check is switched off, an unlisted file has appeared, so the evidence is a pass or fail tied to a named signer and an exact set of files. Unlike the unsigned file hashes kept by data-versioning tools, it shows who stands behind the files, and unlike a watermark, which is trained into the weights so that it survives in an altered copy, it is broken by any change; it says nothing about how the model behaves or what it was trained on.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's machine-learning platform team signs each model at the end of its training pipeline, using the pipeline's own workload identity through Sigstore, and configures its model-serving cluster to load only models whose signature verifies against that identity. Its security team watches the transparency log for signing events under that identity that match no approved release, to decide whether a model reached production outside the release process.

A vehicle maker's perception team downloads a pretrained object detector from a supplier catalogue that signs every model it publishes. Before fine-tuning, it verifies the download against the supplier's published certificate and files the verification output in its supplier-acceptance record, so later reviews can show exactly which files the work started from.

A hospital's imaging department receives quarterly updates to a vendor's chest X-ray triage model. Its clinical engineering team verifies each update against the vendor's certificate and rejects any update whose signature fails, or that contains a file the signature does not cover, before it enters the clinical validation environment.

A public research institute releases an open model together with the test set behind its published benchmark, signing both in one bundle, so that a laboratory re-running the benchmark can confirm that the weights and the test data are byte for byte the ones the institute released before comparing its results with the published ones.

limitations.description: It shows who released the files and that they have not changed, nothing more. A model carrying a malicious pickle payload, a backdoor or the effects of poisoned training data verifies perfectly if its publisher signed it, whether through carelessness or because the publisher's own pipeline was compromised before signing. The originating paper states that signing tells the user nothing about what a model does or how it was produced, so content checks are still needed.

A valid signature is only as good as the consumer's check of who made it. A model signed with an attacker's own identity, or by an account named to look like a well-known organisation (a documented attack on model hubs), verifies cleanly unless the verifier insists on the specific identity, certificate or public key it expects. Consumers need a maintained list of trusted signers for each model source.

A stolen signing key, or a compromised account at the identity provider used for Sigstore signing, produces valid signatures. With Sigstore every signature is recorded in a transparency log, so a publisher that monitors the log for its own identity can spot signatures it did not make; with the key and certificate methods the specification does not require a log entry, so misuse of a key may go unnoticed.

Any change to the files breaks verification, including legitimate ones such as quantisation, conversion to another file format or adding a file. Each derived model needs a new signature from whoever produced it, and that signature says nothing about how the derivative relates to the signed original; recording that relationship needs a separate provenance record, such as the pedigree section of an ML-BOM.

It protects only where verification is enforced. Most models on public hubs are unsigned (fewer than 2% of Hugging Face models used the hub's GPG commit-signing option, per studies the originating paper cites), and an unchecked signature protects nobody. Verification re-hashes every file, and hashing dominates the cost: a 1 TB file took about 13 minutes on a 128-vCPU server in the originating paper's benchmark, which matters if very large models are verified at every load.

techniques.name: Dangerous Capability Evaluation
techniques.description: Dangerous capability evaluation measures whether a frontier AI model can carry out tasks that could enable severe harm, such as finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, persuading or deceiving people, acquiring resources and running copies of itself, or helping to plan an attack with chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear materials, and compares the results with capability thresholds that the developer's safety framework fixes before testing. Evaluators first write a threat model for each risk domain; the framework names a critical capability level, at which the model could pose an extreme risk without extra safeguards, and an early-warning trigger defined on the evaluation results, which the method's originators sketched for one domain as success on more than half of a set of tasks given ten attempts at each. They then build task suites for each domain, such as capture-the-flag hacking challenges in sandboxed networks or multi-step tasks that require the model to set up a cloud server and install software, and try to draw out the model's best performance: it is tested without the safety filters of the deployed product, given agent scaffolding (prompts, planning loops and tools such as a command shell) and sometimes fine-tuned, because the evaluation must not underestimate what the model can do. Scoring records success over repeated attempts and, for tasks the model cannot finish, how close it came, by starting it from intermediate milestones and measuring how much expert help it needs to succeed. Unlike red teaming, which probes a system and its safeguards for whatever failures can be found, and unlike tests of whether a model refuses harmful requests, it measures what the model is able to do, and whether the results cross the trigger informs decisions on deployment and on the security measures the model needs.

example_use_cases.description: A frontier AI developer runs its cyber-offence task suite on each major checkpoint during training and before release, using the agent scaffold its evaluation team has found strongest. Its safety framework sets an early-warning trigger on the share of professional-level capture-the-flag challenges solved; a checkpoint that crosses it cannot be released until stronger protection of the model weights and mitigations against cyber misuse are in place.

A national AI security institute given access to a model before release runs autonomy tasks, such as setting up a cloud server and installing an open-source model on it, both end to end and from intermediate milestones, with a staff member approving each action the agent takes on the live internet. It reports to the developer how close the model came to completing each task and how this compares with the developer's previous model.

A company preparing to publish a model's weights openly evaluates a version fine-tuned on task-relevant data as well as the version it plans to release, because anyone who downloads the weights can fine-tune them, and compares the fine-tuned version's results with its threshold when deciding whether to publish.

limitations.description: A result below the threshold is only as strong as the effort spent drawing out the model's capability. Better scaffolds, more attempts, fine-tuning or a later checkpoint can raise scores, and models can be prompted or fine-tuned to underperform deliberately on dangerous-capability tasks while scoring normally elsewhere, so a negative result is a lower bound on capability, not proof of its absence.

The link between a task score and real-world harm is weakly grounded. The method's originators describe their early-warning trigger as early thinking in an extremely immature area and set no thresholds for their chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear evaluations, where most scientific information is dual-use, so different developers can draw the line in different places and reach different decisions from the same scores.

Task suites cover only the threat models someone has written down, and laboratory tasks may not reflect real conditions: persuasion measured in short dialogues with paid participants, or hacking measured on capture-the-flag challenges, may overstate or understate what the model could do against real people and real systems.

Agentic tasks need sandboxed environments, many repeated runs and expert grading, and tasks with real internet access need a person to approve each action so the agent cannot cause harm, which makes full runs slow and costly. Testing the unfiltered model also needs access that external evaluators may not have; testing the deployed product with its safety filters measures something different.

Results date quickly. Scores change with each new checkpoint and fine-tuning recipe, so evaluations have to be repeated for every significant model update, and published tasks can leak into training data, which is why the originating team withheld solutions and flag values from the tasks it released.

techniques.name: Fault Tree Analysis
techniques.description: Fault tree analysis (FTA) is a deductive, top-down method that starts from one undesired system-level event, such as an automated braking function failing to brake for an obstacle, and works backwards to the combinations of lower-level events that could cause it. The analyst builds a tree of logic gates beneath that top event: an OR gate means any one of its inputs is enough to cause the event above it, an AND gate means all of its inputs must occur together, and the branches end in basic events such as a hardware failure, a human error or a software error. Solving the tree gives its minimal cut sets, the smallest combinations of basic events that produce the top event (a set with a single event is a single point of failure), and, when each basic event has a probability, the probability of the top event, which can be checked against a target or used to set a probability budget for each part. In a system with a machine-learning component, the model's errors enter the tree as basic events of their own, which unlike random hardware failures happen during normal operation at a rate that has to be measured on test or operational data, often depend on conditions such as weather or occlusion that can be added beneath it as conditioning events, and can be correlated from one input to the next. Working down from an acceptable top-event probability turns the model's share into a budget for its error rate, which becomes a performance requirement on the model; the tree shows where model errors matter in the system and how much error it can tolerate, but not why the model makes them.

example_use_cases.description: An avionics team designing an emergency braking system for taxiing aircraft, in which a neural network detects 'No Entry' signs, builds a quantitative fault tree for loss of the restricted-area alert, budgets the detector's misses beside the hardware failures, converts that budget into a maximum per-frame miss probability for the network, and checks on recorded taxi data whether misses in successive frames are independent, as the calculation assumes.

A driving-automation developer analysing the top event 'object not detected in time' adds weather, occlusion and lighting as triggering conditions beneath the camera detector's miss event. Quantifying the tree with rates measured on its own test drives shows which conditions dominate, and it uses the result to decide where a second sensor is needed before widening the vehicle's operating domain.

A hospital pharmacy planning to add a machine-learning dose checker beside pharmacist review draws a tree for 'harmful overdose reaches the patient', with an AND gate requiring both the checker and the pharmacist to miss the error. The analysis shows the claimed risk reduction holds only if the two misses are independent, so the team plans an audit of whether pharmacists check less carefully once the checker is live.

limitations.description: The tree explains only the top events the analysts choose and the causes they think of. Hazards nobody posed as a top event, and losses that arise from interactions between parts that each worked as specified, do not appear, so a fault tree needs a prior hazard identification to decide which top events matter.

A probability for a model-error event is only as good as the data it was measured on. A miss rate estimated on test data holds for the conditions and input mix in that data and changes when the operating environment shifts, so the top-event probability can be badly wrong in conditions the test set under-represents. The main aerospace safety-assessment guidance gives no method for such performance failures, so each assessment has to justify its own.

Quantifying a tree usually assumes basic events are independent, and machine-learning errors often are not: misses on successive camera frames are correlated, and one condition such as fog can degrade a model and the sensor or person meant to back it up at the same time. Unmodelled dependence makes an AND gate look far more protective than it is, so dependence must be checked on data or modelled explicitly.

The model appears in the tree as one or a few basic events, so the analysis says how often the model may err and where its errors matter, not why it errs or which inputs cause the errors. The triggering conditions added beneath a model-error event are only those the analysts already suspect, and finding others needs analysis of the model and its data.

Building and maintaining a tree for a large system is laborious, and it must be revised whenever the architecture or the model changes. Quantification needs a probability for every basic event, and for software, human and model events those numbers are often unavailable or disputed; aviation software guidance, for example, does not accept software reliability rates in the system safety assessment.

techniques.name: System-Theoretic Process Analysis
techniques.description: System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) is a hazard analysis method developed by Nancy Leveson at MIT that treats safety as a control problem: a loss can occur when parts of a system that have not failed interact unsafely, for example when a controller acts on a wrong belief about the process it controls. The analysis has four steps: define the losses to prevent and the system-level hazards that lead to them; model the system as a control structure of controllers, the control actions they issue and the feedback they receive; identify unsafe control actions; and write loss scenarios explaining how each could arise. An unsafe control action is one of four types (not providing an action causes a hazard, providing it causes a hazard, providing it too early, too late or in the wrong order, or stopping it too soon or applying it too long), and loss scenarios cover causes such as missing or wrong feedback, a flawed control algorithm, or a controller's process model (its internal picture of what it controls) that no longer matches reality. In a system with machine-learning components, a learned model appears in the control structure as a controller whose control algorithm and process model were learned from data, or as a feedback source, such as a perception model, whose errors mislead a controller; loss scenarios include training data that missed an operating condition, a shift from training to deployment conditions, and operators who over-rely on the model, and published adaptations also model data collection, training and evaluation as control loops, so that a scenario can trace an unsafe control action back to a development decision such as an incomplete reward function. The output is a traceable set of unsafe control actions, loss scenarios and the safety constraints and requirements derived from them, which the team uses to change the design and to decide what to test; it analyses a model of the system before or alongside testing, and it gives no probabilities.

example_use_cases.description: An automotive supplier building a pedestrian collision-avoidance function around a neural-network detector models the vehicle's control structure with the detector as the braking controller's source of feedback. It finds the unsafe control action 'emergency braking not applied while a pedestrian is crossing', with scenarios such as missed detections of partly hidden pedestrians at dusk, and turns them into requirements on training-data coverage and on the detector's miss rate.

A hospital's patient-safety team preparing to deploy a machine-learning early-warning score for patient deterioration models the score, the nurses who receive its alerts and the doctors who act on them as one control structure. It finds unsafe control actions such as an escalation that comes too late because vital signs reach the record in batches, and alerts ignored after repeated false alarms, and changes data entry and the alerting rules before go-live.

A frontier AI developer's safety team analysing internal use of an AI coding agent models the engineers who prompt it, the automated monitor that scores its sessions, the human reviewers and the merge gate as controllers of the company codebase. It finds unsafe control actions such as a monitoring alert that arrives after the agent's change has been merged, and sets requirements on how quickly sessions are reviewed and on reviewers' independence from the agent.

An engineering team training a reinforcement-learning policy to land a drone splits the mission into approach, descent and touchdown, identifies unsafe control actions for each phase, such as descending too fast close to the landing pad, and uses the loss scenarios to choose the wind and sensor-noise perturbations for its simulation tests and to adjust the reward before the next round of training.

limitations.description: The analysis depends on judgement at every step: deciding which losses matter, where the system ends, which parts act as controllers and which scenarios to record. Separate teams analysing the same system can reach different models and scenario lists, so the work needs review by people outside the team, and a short list of loss scenarios is not evidence that no others exist.

STPA does not estimate how likely a hazard or scenario is, and its authors argue that such estimates are unreliable for software-intensive systems. Where an assurance case or regulator needs a quantitative target, such as a failure rate per hour, it must be paired with a quantitative method, and STPA alone cannot show that a scenario is too rare to need a mitigation.

For a learned component the analysts cannot read the process model or the control algorithm, because both are encoded in trained weights. Scenarios explaining why the model would act unsafely are therefore hypotheses about its training data and operating conditions until tests or monitoring confirm them, and for policies with continuous states and actions the analysis has to be split by mission phase or subtask to stay manageable.

A control structure that covers only the system in operation misses causes that lie in how the model was built, such as data collection, labelling, reward design or the choice of evaluation set; a survey of 31 studies applying STPA to learning-enabled systems found that most modelled operation only. Adding the development lifecycle as control loops finds these causes but makes the analysis substantially larger.

A full analysis of a complex system takes sustained effort from people trained in the method, working with domain and machine-learning experts. A language model can draft loss scenarios faster, but its drafts steer the team towards the scenarios it happens to suggest and can leave gaps, so they need the same review as scenarios written by hand.

techniques.name: Explainer Latency Benchmarking
techniques.description: Explainer latency benchmarking measures how long an explanation method takes to produce an explanation for a single prediction, on the hardware, software and settings it will run with, and compares the result with the time that the decision it supports allows. The evaluator first sets the time budget, the share of the time the decision allows that is left for the explanation once the prediction is ready, then runs the explainer exactly as it will be deployed (the same model, background data, number of samples and batch size) on a representative set of real inputs, timing each explanation from request to a result ready to display, after warm-up runs and with one-off set-up costs, such as building the explainer, recorded separately. Because the time varies with the model, the data, the hardware and the load on the system, each configuration is timed many times, as machine-learning inference benchmarks such as MLPerf Inference time a model, under realistic concurrent demand where the explainer runs as a shared service, and the result is reported as a distribution: the median, high percentiles such as the 95th or 99th, the slowest case and the share of explanations over budget. Canha et al.'s benchmark framework for explanation methods, which scores methods on properties measurable without human participants, includes this property under the name speed and rates it on a five-level scale with cut-offs at 0.1, 1, 5 and 10 seconds aligned with human response-time limits; the scale suits comparisons between methods, while a claim about a deployment needs the measured percentiles set against that deployment's own budget. The output is a latency profile for each explainer configuration, recorded with its hardware, software versions and load, which shows whether explanations will arrive in time and lets a team choose between explainers and settings on speed alongside the explanation quality measured by other tests.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer shows its fraud analysts a feature attribution beside each held transaction and needs it within the two seconds before the review queue refreshes. Benchmarking on the production server at peak queue load, it finds that a sampling-based explainer misses the budget for about one explanation in twenty while an explainer specific to its tree ensemble stays well inside it, and adopts the second once its attributions pass the same faithfulness tests.

A hospital adding an explanation panel to a sepsis-risk alert in its electronic health record agrees with clinicians that the panel must load within one second of a nurse opening the alert. The informatics team times explanations on the hospital's own servers with a week of real alerts at typical volume, reports the 95th percentile and the slowest case against that limit, and repeats the measurement after each model or software update.

An online marketplace shows each seller the main reasons its moderation model held a new listing for review, and the page must update within three seconds. Before launch, the team times the service on its production servers with a week of recorded traffic replayed at its real pace; the first request after each quiet period is far slower because the explainer and its background data load on demand. It keeps a loaded explainer running, re-measures, and reports the slowest case.

limitations.description: Speed and explanation quality trade off through the explainer's settings. Sampling-based explainers run faster with fewer samples or a smaller background dataset, but SHAP's documentation notes that more samples give lower-variance estimates, so a faster setting gives noisier explanations. A latency result holds only for the settings tested, and must be measured at the settings whose faithfulness and stability were checked, or a configuration may meet the budget with untested explanations.

Times depend on the hardware, the implementation and the load at the moment of measurement, which Canha et al. single out as the main caveat on their speed metric, so a figure from a developer's workstation does not carry over to a shared production server or an edge device. Any change to the model, the explainer version, the hardware or the traffic pattern calls for re-measurement, and the configuration must be recorded with the result for it to be checked or repeated.

Claims about the slowest cases need many timed explanations. MLPerf Inference, which sets tail-latency bounds for model inference in the same way, sizes its runs so that a 99th-percentile bound holds with 99 per cent confidence, which at its chosen margin takes about 263,000 queries. A few hundred timings can support a claim about the median but not about the 99th percentile, and a single timed run supports neither.

A fast explanation is not necessarily a good one. Latency says nothing about whether an explanation reflects what the model did or whether people can use it, and it leaves out the time a person needs to read it. It supports a claim about explanations only alongside tests of faithfulness and stability and, where people act on the explanations, a study of whether they can use them within the time available.

The budget has to come from the decision, not from a generic scale. Canha et al.'s cut-offs reflect general limits on human response time, which may be looser or tighter than a particular workflow allows, and a budget that leaves out the time to run the model, move the data and display the result will be met in the benchmark and missed in use; MLPerf likewise derives its server-scenario latency bounds from the user's overall time target.

techniques.name: Kernel Two-Sample Test (Maximum Mean Discrepancy)
techniques.description: A kernel two-sample test checks whether two sets of data could have come from the same distribution; in assurance it is used to check whether the inputs a deployed model now receives still resemble the data on which it was validated, and to detect when they stop doing so. Its statistic, the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), is built from a kernel, a function that scores how similar two data points are (commonly a Gaussian function of the distance between them), and in its usual squared form it is the average similarity among points in the reference sample, plus the average similarity among points in the new sample, minus twice the average similarity between points from different samples. With a characteristic kernel such as the Gaussian, the population value is zero only when the two distributions are identical, so the test can respond to any kind of difference, including a change in how features vary together that tests applied to one feature at a time cannot see, and kernels exist for strings and graphs as well as numerical vectors. To obtain a p-value, the two samples are pooled and repeatedly divided at random into groups of the original sizes, the statistic is recomputed for each division, and the p-value is the share of divisions giving a value at least as large as the one observed; high-dimensional inputs such as images are usually first reduced to a short vector, for example the code of an autoencoder or the model's predicted class probabilities. The output, for each window of new data, is the MMD value and its p-value at a stated significance level, which shows whether that window differs detectably from the reference, but not whether the difference affects the model's accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer's model-risk team tests a random sample of each night's transactions, at most one per customer, against a fixed sample from the fraud model's validation period, after standardising the input features. It set the significance level so that, with nothing changed, it expects about one false alarm a quarter, and a significant result triggers a check of the model's accuracy on newly labelled cases before its alert thresholds are relied on the next day.

Before switching on a chest X-ray triage model at a second hospital that uses a different make of scanner, the deploying team compares 500 recent images from the new site with 500 from the validation set. Each image is first reduced to a short vector by an autoencoder trained on validation images. A significant difference sends the model for local validation on labelled cases from the new site instead of relying on its original results.

A customer-service team whose question-answering assistant was evaluated on a fixed test set compares the sentence embeddings of each week's user questions with those of the test set. When a week is flagged, it computes the MMD witness function, which scores each question by how much more it resembles the new week's questions than the test set, reads the top-scoring questions, finds queries about a new product, and adds such questions to the test set.

limitations.description: A significant result shows that inputs differ from the reference, not that the model has got worse: Rabanser et al. note that distributions shift constantly and often harmlessly, and with large windows the test can flag differences too small to matter. A drift alarm becomes evidence about performance only when followed by an accuracy check on labelled cases, and an absence of alarms reassures only if the test was shown beforehand to detect the shifts that harm the model.

On raw high-dimensional inputs the test has little power: in Rabanser et al.'s comparison on image data the multivariate test performed poorly without first reducing the dimension. The reduction then decides what can be seen, since a change that leaves the autoencoder code or predicted probabilities unchanged goes undetected. The kernel's width matters too: it is usually set to the median distance between points, which Gretton et al. call a heuristic, the best width being an open question.

The statistic compares every pair of points, so its cost grows with the square of the combined sample size, and the permutation test repeats it many times; Rabanser et al. ran kernel tests only up to 1,000 new samples for this reason. Gretton et al.'s linear-time version is far cheaper but needs much more data for the same power, so high-volume monitoring has to trade window size, detection delay and computing cost against each other.

The permutation p-value assumes that observations within each sample are independent. Consecutive sensor readings, transactions from one customer or successive time steps are correlated, and shuffling them breaks that dependence, so the test signals a difference far more often than its stated level: in Chwialkowski et al.'s experiments on autocorrelated signals the permutation test almost always rejected when nothing had changed. Such data need thinning or a wild bootstrap.

Run on every new window at the conventional 5 per cent level, the test flags about one window in twenty even when nothing has changed, which for daily windows means around 18 false alarms a year. Continuous monitoring needs a stricter level, a correction for repeated testing, or an online version of the test whose threshold is set for an expected run time between false alarms.

resources.title: A Kernel Two-Sample Test
resources.abstract: We propose a framework for analyzing and comparing distributions, which we use to construct statistical tests to determine if two samples are drawn from different distributions.  Our test statistic is the largest difference in expectations over functions in the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), and is called the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD).  We present two distribution-free tests based on large deviation bounds for the MMD, and a third test based on the asymptotic distribution of this statistic.  The MMD can be computed in quadratic time, although efficient linear time approximations are available.  Our statistic is an instance of an integral probability metric, and various classical metrics on distributions are obtained when alternative function classes are used in place of an RKHS.  We apply our two-sample tests  to a variety of problems, including attribute matching for databases using the Hungarian marriage method, where they perform strongly.  Excellent performance is also obtained when comparing distributions over graphs, for which these are the first such tests.

Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
resources.abstract: We might hope that when faced with unexpected inputs, well-designed software systems would fire off warnings. Machine learning (ML) systems, however, which depend strongly on properties of their inputs (e.g. the i.i.d. assumption), tend to fail silently. This paper explores the problem of building ML systems that fail loudly, investigating methods for detecting dataset shift, identifying exemplars that most typify the shift, and quantifying shift malignancy. We focus on several datasets and various perturbations to both covariates and label distributions with varying magnitudes and fractions of data affected. Interestingly, we show that across the dataset shifts that we explore, a two-sample-testing-based approach, using pre-trained classifiers for dimensionality reduction, performs best. Moreover, we demonstrate that domain-discriminating approaches tend to be helpful for characterizing shifts qualitatively and determining if they are harmful.

techniques.name: Appropriate Reliance Measurement
techniques.description: Appropriate reliance measurement tests whether people who receive an AI system's advice follow it when it is right and keep their own judgement when it is wrong, and whether an explanation, or another aid such as a confidence score, moves them towards that pattern. It uses a two-step decision study on a classification task, the only kind Schemmer et al. define it for: for each task item the participant first decides alone, then sees the AI's advice, with or without the explanation, and makes a final decision, on a set of items with known correct answers drawn so that the AI is wrong on a known share of them. Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree are counted, because when they agree the final decision cannot show which source the person relied on. Schemmer et al. define two rates over these items: relative AI reliance, the share of items with a wrong first decision and correct advice on which the person switched to the advice, and relative self-reliance, the share of items with a correct first decision and wrong advice on which the person kept their own answer. Comparing the two rates between an explanation condition and a control condition shows whether the explanation reduces under-reliance (rejecting correct advice), reduces over-reliance (accepting wrong advice) or merely raises agreement with the AI, which overall accuracy or agreement with the AI does not show on its own.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer considering highlighted claim features as an explanation for its fraud-flagging model runs a two-step study with its claims handlers on 40 past claims, with the model wrong on a quarter of them, comparing handlers who see the flag alone with handlers who also see the highlights. It adopts the highlights only if relative AI reliance rises without relative self-reliance falling, since higher acceptance of all advice, right and wrong, would show deference rather than better judgement.

A conservation charity whose volunteers identify bird species with help from an image classifier measures relative AI reliance and relative self-reliance separately for experienced birders and beginners, and for example-based and written explanations. It chooses which explanation to show each group from the results, because a volunteer's expertise changes how an explanation, especially a wrong one, shifts their reliance on the classifier.

A hospital whose safety case for a sepsis alert relies on ward doctors overriding wrong alerts, and whose workflow has doctors record their own escalation decision before the alert appears, runs a vignette study in that workflow, with and without the alert's explanation panel. Before switching the panel on, it reports relative self-reliance, and the share of wrong-alert cases that ended in a wrong decision, against the oversight requirement in the safety case.

limitations.description: The rates describe behaviour on a task set built to contain many AI errors: Schemmer et al. drew equal numbers of items from each cell of the confusion matrix, which put the AI's accuracy on their 16 items at 50%. The study does not show how people rely on advice when errors are rarer, as they usually are in service, so it supports a claim about the conditions tested, not a direct estimate of over-reliance in deployment.

Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree enter the two rates, so each rate can rest on a handful of items per person, and items on which the person and the AI are wrong together, the errors that oversight cannot catch, enter neither rate. Plan the sample around the expected number of disagreements, and report beside the rates the share of wrong-advice items that ended in a wrong final decision.

Asking for a decision before the advice is shown is itself an intervention. Guo et al.'s reanalysis of an earlier study found reliance closer to the appropriate level when people decided first than when they saw the AI's advice first, so a two-step study may show better reliance than a deployed system that presents the advice straight away.

The rates judge each decision by whether the advice turned out to be right, not by whether following it was the better bet given what the person could see. Guo et al. argue that this outcome-based definition mixes two failures, wrong beliefs about how often the AI is right and poor use of those beliefs, and treats a close call the same as an obvious one, so a low rate does not say which to fix.

Results depend on who takes part and on how good the explanations are. Morrison et al. found that participants' expertise changed how incorrect explanations affected their reliance, and that example-based explanations misled participants more than written ones, so a result from novices, or from explanations that were always correct, does not carry over to expert users or to explanations that are sometimes wrong.

techniques.name: Explanation Satisfaction Scale
techniques.description: The Explanation Satisfaction Scale is a short questionnaire on which people who have used an AI system's explanations rate how satisfying and sufficient they found them; Hoffman, Mueller, Klein and Litman developed it in the DARPA Explainable AI programme to capture the user's judgement of an explanation, as distinct from a researcher's judgement of its quality. Each item is a statement about the explanation, for example that from it the user understands how the system works, or that it is satisfying, has sufficient detail, seems complete, tells the user how to use the system, is useful to their goals or shows how accurate the system is, and each is rated on a five-point scale from 'I agree strongly' to 'I disagree strongly'. Participants complete it after they have worked with the system and received explanations, usually once for each explanation condition in a study that compares conditions; the published form sets no scoring rule or threshold, and the implementation by one of its authors in the OpenScales library scores it as the mean of the item ratings. Versions differ: the authors' 2018 report gives eight items, their 2023 journal article seven (it drops the item on knowing when to trust the system), and the form on the XAITK site nine (it adds an item on reliability), with a note that researchers may use a subset. The score measures how users judge an explanation, not whether they understood it or decide better with it, and the authors present it beside separate measures of mental models, trust and task performance.

example_use_cases.description: A research team comparing counterfactual images with saliency heatmaps (LIME and layer-wise relevance propagation) for a chest X-ray pneumonia classifier gives lay participants the scale after they have predicted the classifier's decision on a set of images. It chooses which explanation to develop on prediction accuracy and uses the ratings only as a second check, so that the explanation people prefer is not assumed to be the one they understand better.

A team deciding whether causal explanations of a reinforcement-learning agent's strategy in a real-time strategy game are worth the extra modelling gives participants the scale after each explained gameplay video. It compares the causal explanations with a simpler explanation and with no explanation on four items (understanding, satisfaction, sufficient detail and completeness), and pairs the ratings with a test of whether participants can predict the agent's next action.

A lender piloting a new letter that explains which factors led to a credit refusal asks pilot applicants to complete the scale after reading either the new letter or the current one. It uses the items on sufficient detail and usefulness to decide whether to add the sentence, held back so far, that says what change would have led to approval.

limitations.description: A high rating does not show that people understand the system or decide better with it. Hase and Bansal found no evidence that participants' ratings of explanation quality predicted whether the explanations helped them predict the model, Buçinca et al. found that subjective measures did not predict performance on the real decision task, and the scale's authors note that people can feel satisfied while their understanding is piecemeal or wrong.

The published evidence for the scale is small: content-validity ratings by 35 attendees of a DARPA programme meeting, an internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) of 0.86, and eight volunteers rating good and bad explanations of everyday technologies, where the difference was large but only marginally significant. The 2018 report's mean for good explanations (42.75) exceeds what eight items scored 1 to 5 can sum to, so the form tested is unclear, and the XAITK page asks for reliability data.

There are no norms or thresholds, so a score means something only against another condition in the same study, such as the current explanation or no explanation. A mean rating reported on its own, such as 4 out of 5, cannot support a claim that an explanation is satisfactory.

Versions with seven, eight and nine items are in circulation, item wording differs between them, and the form invites researchers to use a subset; Madumal et al., for example, report four items. Scores from different studies are therefore not comparable unless the same items and wording were used, and each study should report exactly which it used.

resources.abstract: The question addressed in this paper is: If we present to a user an AI system that explains how it works, how do we know whether the explanation works and the user has achieved a pragmatic understanding of the AI? In other words, how do we know that an explanainable AI system (XAI) is any good? Our focus is on the key concepts of measurement. We discuss specific methods for evaluating: (1) the goodness of explanations, (2) whether users are satisfied by explanations, (3) how well users understand the AI systems, (4) how curiosity motivates the search for explanations, (5) whether the user's trust and reliance on the AI are appropriate, and finally, (6) how the human-XAI work system performs. The recommendations we present derive from our integration of extensive research literatures and our own psychometric evaluations.

techniques.name: Forward Simulation Test
techniques.description: A forward simulation test checks whether people who have studied a model's explanations can predict the model's output for inputs they have not seen, so it tests with people the understanding an explanation method is assumed to give, where fidelity checks only compare the explanation with the model by computation. Doshi-Velez and Kim proposed it as a human-grounded evaluation of interpretability: participants are given an explanation and an input and must state what the model will output, whether or not that output is correct. In the controlled design of Hase and Bansal, participants study a set of examples with the model's outputs, predict the outputs for a separate set of test inputs, then study the same examples with explanations added and predict the same test inputs again, and the gain in accuracy is credited to the explanations (a separate group that studies the examples without explanations guards against a practice gain); the test inputs are kept apart from the explained examples so that explanations cannot give the answers away, and are chosen so that the model is right and wrong equally often, so that predicting the true label scores no better than chance. A counterfactual variant, in Hase and Bansal's form, shows an input, the model's output and its explanation, and asks what the model will output for an edited version of that input, with edits chosen so that half change the output. The result is the change in the share of correct predictions, with a confidence interval, for each explanation method or design compared; it is evidence that people can anticipate the model on the kind of input tested, not that they make better decisions with it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team must choose between feature-attribution bar charts and a short rule list as the explanation shown to credit analysts for a loan-default model. It runs a forward simulation test with 30 credit analysts on past applications, balanced between correct and incorrect model predictions, and adopts the rule list only if its gain over the no-explanation baseline is clearly larger than that of the bar charts; otherwise it treats the two as equal.

An online platform's trust and safety team uses the counterfactual variant to test whether moderators who see which words a toxicity classifier weighted can predict whether it will still flag a comment after one of those words is replaced. A score no better than the baseline tells the team that the highlights do not show how the classifier responds to edits, before it writes moderation guidance that relies on them.

A research team choosing between counterfactual images and saliency heatmaps for a chest X-ray pneumonia classifier shows each group of participants explained example images, then asks them to predict the classifier's decision on 12 other images, three from each cell of its confusion matrix, without explanations. It takes forward to a study with clinicians the explanation whose group predicts best, measured against a group that saw the examples without explanations.

A local authority plans to show caseworkers, who are outside the team that built it, the reasons behind a housing-benefit fraud-risk score. Before releasing the reasons in that form, it runs a forward simulation test with caseworkers on unseen cases, half of them cases the score got wrong, using the reasons exactly as they will appear, and revises them if caseworkers who studied them predict the flag no better than caseworkers who did not.

limitations.description: A pass shows that people can anticipate the model, not that they decide better with it. Buçinca et al. found that results on a task of predicting an AI's decisions did not predict results on the real decision task, and Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al. found that people who could better simulate a simple, clear model did not follow it more when that helped, and in some experiments were less able to correct its large mistakes. A claim about decisions needs a decision study.

The test is easily made trivial. If the explained examples are reused as test items, explanations that show the predicted class or a probability give the answer away, and if the model is mostly right, participants can score well by predicting the true label. Hase and Bansal found earlier studies that reused the same items for explanation and prediction; results from such designs overstate what the explanation conveys.

Effects are often small against the variation between people and items. With 32 trained undergraduates and about 180 to 320 responses per condition, Hase and Bansal's 95% confidence intervals on the change in accuracy were about 8 to 13 percentage points either side, and only LIME on tabular data clearly improved both forward and counterfactual simulation. A study must be sized for the difference it needs to detect, with a bootstrap over both participants and items.

The score holds for the people tested. Many studies use students or crowd workers because domain experts are costly to recruit, which Doshi-Velez and Kim give as the reason this kind of evaluation is cheaper; a result from lay participants does not show that the clinicians, analysts or caseworkers who will use the explanation can predict the model.

The before-and-after design credits any gain to the explanations, but participants see the same examples and test items twice, and Hase and Bansal had no group that repeated both phases without explanations, so a practice gain is not ruled out. Their participants also found it hard to remember the explained examples while predicting, so the number of examples and the time allowed must be fixed and reported when methods are compared.

resources.title: Towards A Rigorous Science of Interpretable Machine Learning
resources.abstract: As machine learning systems become ubiquitous, there has been a surge of interest in interpretable machine learning: systems that provide explanation for their outputs. These explanations are often used to qualitatively assess other criteria such as safety or non-discrimination. However, despite the interest in interpretability, there is very little consensus on what interpretable machine learning is and how it should be measured. In this position paper, we first define interpretability and describe when interpretability is needed (and when it is not). Next, we suggest a taxonomy for rigorous evaluation and expose open questions towards a more rigorous science of interpretable machine learning.

techniques.name: Think-Aloud Study of Explanation Use
techniques.description: A think-aloud study of explanation use asks a small number of participants to say what they are thinking while they use an AI system's explanations to do a realistic task, so that the design team can see how the explanation is read, used, ignored or misread. It applies the think-aloud method from cognitive psychology, which rests on Ericsson and Simon's account of verbal reports: people can voice what they are attending to as they work without changing their thinking, provided they are not asked to report things they would not otherwise attend to, such as the reasons for their actions. In a session, a facilitator gives a short practice task, then sets tasks in which the participant sees the model's output and explanation and makes a decision, and while the participant works gives only neutral reminders, such as 'what are you thinking?', when they fall silent; audio and screen are recorded. The recordings are transcribed and coded, often by thematic analysis, into findings such as parts of the explanation that were misread, parts never looked at and questions it left unanswered, and the team changes the design and tests it again. The output is qualitative, design-stage evidence about how an explanation is understood: it can show that a misreading occurs, but not how often it occurs among users or whether their decisions improve.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a nurse-facing explanation for a patient deterioration score runs think-aloud sessions with six ward nurses on a clickable prototype using past patient records. It finds that nurses read a factor that lowered the score as a sign that the patient was improving, relabels the chart, and re-tests the new labels in a second round before fixing the design for a quantitative evaluation.

The developer of a vocal emotion-recognition app that highlights which parts of a recording drove each prediction runs remote think-aloud sessions with a dozen users. One participant reads the highlight colour bar as a trace of the speaker's tone of voice, a misreading that no rating of the explanation would have revealed, and the team changes how the highlight is drawn.

A bank's model risk team preparing to give loan officers counterfactual explanations (for example, the income at which a refused application would have been approved) runs think-aloud sessions with five officers on past applications, including some the model got wrong. It learns which suggestions officers would pass on to applicants and which they reject as implausible, and decides whether to filter the suggestions before release.

limitations.description: How participants are asked to talk changes what is observed. A meta-analysis of 94 studies by Fox, Ericsson and Best found that plain thinking aloud left accuracy unchanged, but that asking people to explain or describe their thinking changed performance, and that verbal reports of every kind tended to make tasks take longer. Facilitators must avoid 'why' prompts, and task times from these sessions cannot serve as performance measures.

Talking through a task can make people attend to an explanation more than they would at work. In Buçinca et al.'s think-aloud study, participants' preferences between two explanation types matched the results of a proxy task rather than those of the realistic task, and the authors suggest thinking aloud pushed people into analytical thinking, so these sessions may overstate how closely users read explanations in normal use.

Studies use few participants (between 4 and 14 in the sources for this record), so a finding shows that a problem exists, not how common it is, and cannot support a claim about the share of users who understand an explanation or about decision quality. The sessions also show only the situations their tasks include: tasks need some wrong model outputs if the team wants to see how people use an explanation when the model errs.

Not everything people do with an explanation gets said. Quick, perceptual uses leave little trace: in Zhang and Lim's study, participants called the audio examples intuitive but did not say why they found them simple. People also tend to say what they think the right answer is, the social desirability bias the GOV.UK guidance warns of. Silence about part of an explanation does not mean it went unused or was understood, and a screen recording or gaze data is needed to tell these apart.

Findings depend on the analyst: coding transcripts into themes is interpretive, so a study meant to support an assurance claim needs a stated coding scheme and a second coder. The voice and screen recordings are personal data that need participants' consent and controlled storage, and recordings made on real cases may also hold personal data about the people those cases concern.

techniques.name: AI FactSheets
techniques.description: AI FactSheets is a documentation practice in which the developer or supplier of an AI model or service answers a structured set of questions about it, modelled on the supplier's declarations of conformity that industries such as telecommunications and transport use to give written assurance, with evidence, that a product meets stated requirements. The questions cover the service's purpose and its intended and unsuitable uses, the datasets it was trained and tested on, its test methods and results (reported for groups such as age bands or genders where relevant), checks for bias, explainability, behaviour on data unlike its training data and robustness to adversarial attack, how user data is secured, and its lineage, such as when and how its models were retrained; 'N/A' and 'Proprietary' are allowed answers. Facts are gathered from the people in each role across the lifecycle (business owner, data scientist, model validator and operations engineer), and any change to the service produces a new version of the FactSheet while earlier versions are kept. The originating group's seven-step method designs the template with its readers: interview the people who will read the facts and those who will produce them, draft and trial a template of questions, have the real producers complete it, evaluate the result with its readers for content and presentation, and build further templates for other audiences such as a review board or regulator. Unlike a model card, which reports one model's intended use and evaluation to the people choosing it, or a datasheet, which describes one dataset, a FactSheet may cover one model or a whole service built from several models and datasets (attaching their datasheets), gathers facts from each role in the lifecycle and has a different template for each audience; unlike a CycloneDX ML-BOM it is written for people to read rather than as a machine-readable parts list for software tools.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital trust buying a speech-to-text service for clinical dictation sends bidders a FactSheet template asking for intended and unsuitable uses, training data, retraining frequency, behaviour on noisy audio, and word error rates by speaker accent and age band on recordings the trust supplies. The panel compares the answers to shortlist bidders, re-tests the shortlisted services on its own recordings, and writes the confirmed error rates into the contract as service levels.

A bank's model risk team follows the seven-step method to design a FactSheet template for credit models: it interviews validators about the decisions they make and data scientists about the facts they can record, then has the scientists complete it for a new affordability model. Validators read the completed FactSheet's training data, performance, bias checks and known weak cases before deciding whether to approve the model for deployment.

A company selling a sentiment-analysis API publishes a short FactSheet for developers browsing its catalogue, giving the purpose, input and output formats, training data, accuracy and the kinds of text the service handles poorly. From the same facts it generates a longer FactSheet, with a different template, for enterprise customers' risk and compliance reviewers.

A city council's AI ethics review board asks each supplier for a FactSheet in a template written for the board, covering training and test data distributions, data handling, the inputs the service handles poorly and possible sources of unfair outcomes. The board reads them before deciding whether a photo-based street-repair reporting service may go live.

limitations.description: A FactSheet is the supplier's own declaration. As with the declarations of conformity it imitates, the supplier runs the tests it reports and nothing in the format checks them, so it shows what was claimed rather than that the claims hold. A buyer who relies on a declared figure has to re-test the service or ask for third-party testing, which the original proposal expects only for the highest-stakes, regulated, enterprise and public-sector applications.

Facts not recorded while the service is built are hard to recover. In IBM's own trials, developers forgot how they had transformed training data or which settings they had tried, and recovering the training-data transformations for one FactSheet took several hours over two days although the dataset was small and its author was available. A FactSheet written after development is likely to have gaps or errors unless fact collection is part of the development process.

The format accepts 'N/A' and 'Proprietary' as answers. In IBM's trials most developers assumed bias would not be an issue and marked bias questions not applicable, even where further questioning showed it could be, and participants were unsure how much detail they could give without losing competitive advantage. An unchallenged 'N/A' can hide a risk nobody examined, and items withheld as proprietary are often the ones a buyer would need in order to check the self-declared results.

There is no single FactSheet. Its authors hold that one template cannot serve every audience and domain, and developers report the metrics conventional for their kind of model, so FactSheets from different suppliers often cannot be compared unless the buyer fixes the questions, metrics and test conditions in its own template.

Whether readers understand FactSheets and decide better with them is untested. Producers in IBM's studies found it hard to know what readers needed and often left out what a less expert reader would need. The design method checks a draft with a few intended readers, and the group's later case studies report that producers could follow it, but none of these sources tests whether buyers, validators or review boards read FactSheets correctly or make better decisions with them.

resources.title: A Methodology for Creating AI FactSheets
resources.abstract: As AI models and services are used in a growing number of highstakes areas, a consensus is forming around the need for a clearer record of how these models and services are developed to increase trust. Several proposals for higher quality and more consistent AI documentation have emerged to address ethical and legal concerns and general social impacts of such systems. However, there is little published work on how to create this documentation. This is the first work to describe a methodology for creating the form of AI documentation we call FactSheets. We have used this methodology to create useful FactSheets for nearly two dozen models. This paper describes this methodology and shares the insights we have gathered. Within each step of the methodology, we describe the issues to consider and the questions to explore with the relevant people in an organization who will be creating and consuming the AI facts in a FactSheet. This methodology will accelerate the broader adoption of transparent AI documentation.
